triage.name: Varicocele
triage.reason: Scrotal swelling with a characteristic bag-of-worms exam finding; diagnosed clinically and by ultrasound, with infertility implications.

demographics: Present in about 15% of adult men and up to 20% of adolescents
More often detected on the left side
A common finding in men evaluated for infertility

risk_factors.text: Male infertility or abnormal semen analysis

family_history: Varicocele in a father or brother

chief_complaints.text: I feel a heavy, achy feeling in my scrotum
There's a lump on the left side of my scrotum
My scrotum looks different — like there are worms under the skin
We've been trying to have a baby and it hasn't happened

hpi.onset: Gradual; often noticed incidentally or during adolescence
hpi.progression: Slowly enlarges over time; may become more noticeable with standing or straining
hpi.location: Left side of the scrotum in most cases; can be bilateral
hpi.radiation: May radiate along the spermatic cord toward the groin
hpi.quality: Dull, dragging ache or heaviness; the swelling feels like a bag of worms
hpi.timing: Worse after standing, prolonged activity or at the end of the day; improves when lying down

associated_symptoms.text: Noticeable swelling that shrinks when lying down
Smaller testicle on the affected side
Difficulty achieving pregnancy with a partner

atypical.how_it_differs: Prepubertal boys rarely have varicoceles; when present, consider a retroperitoneal mass or other secondary cause.
A new varicocele in an older man, especially on the right or that does not shrink when lying down, raises concern for a retroperitoneal or renal mass.
Scrotal examination can be difficult, so the varicocele may be missed or only detected on ultrasound.

general.moderate: Mild discomfort when standing; otherwise comfortable
general.severe: Visible scrotal enlargement with a dragging ache; may sit or adjust posture to relieve it
general.critical: Not applicable; varicocele is not a critical illness

findings.maneuver: Palpate the spermatic cord between the thumb and index finger
Ask the patient to stand and perform a Valsalva maneuver while palpating the cord
findings.finding: Swelling and tortuosity increase with Valsalva

findings.maneuver: Have the patient lie down and re-examine the scrotum
findings.finding: The swelling decreases or disappears when supine

findings.maneuver: Compare the size and consistency of both testes
findings.finding: Smaller, softer testis on the affected side

findings.maneuver: Examine both sides of the scrotum
findings.finding: Abnormality confined to the left side
No redness or warmth of the scrotal skin

findings.maneuver: Palpate the inguinal canal and ask the patient to cough
findings.finding: No inguinal bulge or expansile cough impulse

labs.caveat: Not applicable in men; listed only to note that pregnancy testing has no role in this condition.

imaging.preferred_when: First-line imaging for any suspected varicocele, especially when the exam is equivocal, the patient is obese, or the varicocele is right-sided or new

findings.text: Dilated, tortuous veins of the pampiniform plexus measuring more than 3 mm in diameter
Venous dilation that increases with Valsalva maneuver and decreases when supine
Retrograde venous flow on color Doppler during Valsalva
Smaller testicular volume on the affected side
Normal testicular parenchyma without a discrete mass

No obstructing mass in the typical primary varicocele

imaging.study: MRI abdomen and pelvis without contrast

decision_points: A varicocele that does not shrink when the patient lies down, is right-sided, or appears new in an older man should prompt imaging for a retroperitoneal or renal mass.
Semen analysis is offered when infertility is a concern or before surgical repair.
Scrotal ultrasound is used when the physical exam is equivocal, the patient is obese, or the varicocele is not typical.

differential.name: Testicular torsion
differential.why_considered: Acute scrotal pain and swelling can be mistaken for a symptomatic varicocele
differential.trigger: Sudden severe testicular pain with a high-riding, transversely lying testis and absent cremasteric reflex

history: Sudden onset of severe pain, often waking the patient from sleep
exam: High-riding testis with horizontal lie
Absent cremasteric reflex
Diffuse testicular tenderness without a bag-of-worms cord
labs: No specific laboratory finding; diagnosis is clinical and surgical
imaging: Reduced or absent testicular blood flow on color Doppler ultrasound

differential.name: Epididymitis
differential.why_considered: Scrotal pain and swelling are common to both conditions
differential.trigger: Gradual-onset unilateral scrotal pain with fever, dysuria, or urethral discharge

history: Gradual onset over hours to days
Dysuria, urinary frequency, or urethral discharge
Sexually transmitted infection risk or recent urinary instrumentation
exam: Tenderness localized to the epididymis, especially the tail
Scrotal erythema and warmth
Positive Prehn sign (pain relief with scrotal elevation) is unreliable but may be present
labs: Positive nucleic acid amplification test for Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoeae
imaging: Enlarged, hyperemic epididymis on Doppler ultrasound
Normal or reactive hydrocele; no dilated pampiniform plexus veins

differential.name: Inguinal hernia
differential.why_considered: A groin or scrotal bulge can resemble a varicocele

history: Bulge that is more prominent with coughing, straining, or standing
May be reducible when lying down
Discomfort with lifting or prolonged standing
exam: Palpable inguinal bulge with an expansile cough impulse
Bowel sounds may be audible over the hernia
The swelling is separate from the spermatic cord and does not feel like a bag of worms
imaging: Ultrasound or CT shows bowel or omentum in the inguinal canal

differential.name: Testicular cancer
differential.why_considered: A painless testicular mass or swelling may be attributed to a varicocele
differential.trigger: Firm, painless intratesticular mass or new testicular enlargement

history: No change with position or Valsalva
May have a history of cryptorchidism
exam: Firm, irregular intratesticular mass that does not transilluminate
Testis may be enlarged rather than atrophic
No bag-of-worms cord
labs: Elevated alpha-fetoprotein, beta-hCG, or lactate dehydrogenase

differential.name: Spermatocele
differential.why_considered: A scrotal mass can be confused with a varicocele

history: Painless or mildly uncomfortable scrotal lump
Does not change with position or Valsalva
exam: Cystic, transilluminating mass separate from the testis, usually at the epididymal head
No tortuous cord
imaging: Cystic lesion on ultrasound without venous dilation

differential.name: Hydrocele
differential.why_considered: Scrotal swelling is a shared feature

history: May fluctuate with activity but does not shrink when lying down
exam: Fluid-filled scrotal swelling that transilluminates
Testis may be difficult to palpate
No bag-of-worms cord
imaging: Anechoic fluid collection around the testis on ultrasound

differential.name: Varicocele secondary to retroperitoneal mass
differential.why_considered: A new or non-decompressing varicocele may be the presenting sign of a retroperitoneal or renal tumor obstructing the gonadal vein
differential.trigger: Right-sided varicocele, new varicocele in an older man, or a varicocele that does not shrink when supine

history: New scrotal swelling in an older man
Constitutional symptoms such as weight loss, night sweats, or flank pain
exam: Varicocele that does not decompress when lying down
Palpable abdominal or flank mass
Right-sided varicocele
labs: Anemia or elevated inflammatory markers may be present
imaging: CT or MRI shows a retroperitoneal or renal mass compressing the gonadal vein

severity.mild: Small, palpable only with Valsalva; no pain, normal testicular size, and no fertility concerns
severity.moderate: Palpable at rest, visible bag-of-worms, mild to moderate scrotal discomfort, and possible mild testicular asymmetry
severity.severe: Large, visibly distended scrotum with persistent pain, marked testicular atrophy, and abnormal semen parameters
severity.critical: Not applicable; varicocele is not a life-threatening condition

red_flags.finding: Sudden severe testicular pain with nausea and vomiting
red_flags.meaning: Suggests testicular torsion, a surgical emergency

red_flags.finding: Right-sided varicocele or one that does not shrink when lying down
red_flags.meaning: Raises concern for a retroperitoneal or renal mass obstructing the gonadal vein

red_flags.finding: New varicocele in an older man
red_flags.meaning: May indicate a secondary cause such as a retroperitoneal tumor
Suggests testicular cancer rather than a varicocele
Points toward epididymitis or another infectious process

complications.name: Testicular atrophy
clues: Smaller, softer testis on the affected side

complications.name: Male infertility
clues: Difficulty achieving pregnancy with a partner

complications.name: Chronic scrotal pain
clues: Dull, dragging ache that worsens with standing and improves with lying down

complications.name: Hydrocele
clues: Fluid collection around the testis on ultrasound

special_populations.differences: Prepubertal boys rarely have varicoceles; when present, consider a retroperitoneal mass or other secondary cause. Adolescent varicoceles may affect testicular growth and warrant monitoring.
A new varicocele in an older man, especially on the right or that does not shrink when lying down, raises concern for a retroperitoneal or renal mass and should prompt imaging.
Scrotal examination can be difficult, so the varicocele may be missed or only detected on ultrasound.

key_questions.question: What does the scrotal swelling or discomfort feel like, and when did you first notice it?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual onset of a dull, dragging ache or heaviness over months to years, not sudden severe pain

key_questions.question: Does the swelling or ache change when you stand up, strain, or lie down?
key_questions.looking_for: Worse with standing, exertion, or Valsalva and better or gone when lying down — the positional pattern of a varicocele

key_questions.question: Which side is affected — left, right, or both?
key_questions.looking_for: Left-sided predominance; right-sided or bilateral raises concern for a secondary cause

key_questions.question: Have you or your partner had trouble getting pregnant, or has anyone said your sperm count is low?
key_questions.looking_for: Infertility or abnormal semen analysis, the main reason varicoceles are treated

key_questions.question: Have you noticed one testicle looking or feeling smaller than the other?
key_questions.looking_for: Testicular atrophy or asymmetry on the affected side

key_questions.question: Is there any pain, and if so, how severe is it and does it interfere with daily activities?
key_questions.looking_for: Mild to moderate dull ache; severe or acute pain suggests another diagnosis

key_questions.question: Any fever, burning with urination, or discharge from the penis?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; if present, points toward epididymitis or another infection

key_questions.question: Have you had any scrotal surgery, trauma, or prior groin hernia repair?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior instrumentation or surgery that could explain the swelling

key_questions.question: Has anyone in your family had a varicocele or fertility problems?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history of varicocele or male infertility

key_questions.question: Have you had any unintentional weight loss, night sweats, or flank or back pain?
key_questions.looking_for: Constitutional or flank symptoms suggesting a retroperitoneal or renal mass causing a secondary varicocele

key_questions.question: Are you sexually active, and have you had any sexually transmitted infections?
key_questions.looking_for: STI risk factors that would point toward epididymitis rather than varicocele

reasoning_points: Gradual onset of a dull, dragging scrotal ache or heaviness that worsens with standing or straining and improves when lying down
Left-sided predominance, consistent with the anatomy of the left gonadal vein draining into the left renal vein
Palpable bag-of-worms thickening of the spermatic cord that augments with Valsalva and decompresses when supine
No fever, dysuria, urethral discharge, or scrotal erythema to suggest infection
No sudden severe pain or absent cremasteric reflex to suggest testicular torsion
Scrotal ultrasound with color Doppler showing dilated pampiniform plexus veins greater than 3 mm with retrograde flow on Valsalva
Semen analysis and testicular size assessed when infertility or testicular atrophy is a concern
Right-sided, non-decompressing, or new varicocele in an older man prompts imaging for a retroperitoneal or renal mass

easy: Adolescent or young adult man with a classic left-sided bag-of-worms cord that augments with Valsalva and decompresses when supine
Dull dragging ache worse at the end of the day and relieved by lying down
No fever, dysuria, or acute severe pain
Scrotal ultrasound confirms dilated pampiniform plexus veins
medium: Man evaluated for infertility with an incidental varicocele and abnormal semen analysis
Obese patient in whom the varicocele is not palpable and is only found on ultrasound
Bilateral or right-sided varicocele requiring imaging to exclude a secondary cause
Mild chronic scrotal pain with a normal urinalysis and no infectious symptoms
hard: New right-sided varicocele in an older man that does not decompress when supine, suggesting a retroperitoneal or renal mass
Prepubertal boy with a varicocele, raising concern for a secondary cause
Patient presenting with acute scrotal pain where torsion must be excluded first
Varicocele coexisting with a hydrocele or inguinal hernia that obscures the classic findings
